title: An uploaded file is a stream, and there is one way to receive it
scope:
how an uploaded file reaches an application and what bounds it — the single receiving
accessor, what a part is, the three ways to consume one, where a stream reaches disk, and the two caps
that replace one. Not in scope: the raw request body, which stays
[0097](0097.md) § 8; how a multipart message's *spelling* is read,
including the part-count cap, which stays
[0095](0095.md); what `tainted` means and where it must be
laundered ([0024](0024.md)); the changeability classes the two caps
are instances of ([0005](0005.md)); and everything else about the server
([0097](0097.md)).

[0097](0097.md) — § 8 is the decision this one

summary.headline: An uploaded file is a stream, and there is one way to receive it
summary.body:
`Core\Request::files()` yields uploaded parts lazily, one at a time as they arrive, and it is
the only way to receive an uploaded file; there is no array of finished uploads. A part is
consumed in one of three ways: read whole, bounded by the request body cap; iterated as chunks
of bytes; or written straight to disk. Peak memory for an upload of any size is one chunk per
in-flight request. `request_body` bounds what is parsed into memory and `upload_total` bounds a
streamed multipart body. There is no temporary file.
